scopeReview: PSO-3.A.1–3: shared transmitted practices/technologies/attitudes/behavior; food, architecture, land use; ethnocentrism and cultural relativism. Avoids biological determinism, uniform-group stereotypes and conflating contextual understanding with unconditional ethical approval. June2026 clarifications do not alter this topic scope.
varietyReview: Field-note classification table, one-trait architecture map, within-society age/practice chart and observer-attitude table. Other tasks address technology/norms, resources/preferences, neutral inquiry, continuity/change, political boundaries and sampling. All five skills, mixed difficulty and varied keys.
repetitionReview: New cultural constructs distinguish these from Unit1 data methods: contextual interpretation versus ranking, shared technology versus physical statistic and internal cultural variation. Sampling and scale are applied to cultural claims rather than repeating prior stems or data.
referenceNote: Primary curriculum and UNESCO cultural-transmission context; original invented communities/statements/data. No copied activity, named-group stereotypes or student resource additions. No independent human review claimed.

questions.independentReview: Classified transmission mechanisms in supplied notes: recipe taught, etiquette taught, rainfall measured. Interaction between environment and culture does not turn a climate statistic itself into a learned norm.

questions.correctOption: Describe a north–south difference in courtyard use while recognizing that one trait does not define every cultural characteristic.
questions.independentReview: Compared north80/70 to south25/20, all nonzero and below100. Interpreted a single measured trait, avoiding whole-culture or individual-identity inference from aggregate shading.

questions.correctOption: Practices vary within this society, and the one-time data do not prove that individuals never change their preparation.
questions.independentReview: Checked each pair sums100 and each preparation appears in all three groups. Observations are cross-sectional, so differences by age do not establish individual constancy or a transmission mechanism.

questions.correctOption: A uses an ethnocentric judgment; B seeks contextual understanding associated with cultural relativism.
questions.independentReview: Compared the actual basis of interpretation: A treats home practice as the universal standard; B investigates local meanings. Kept cultural relativism distinct from asserting identical cultures or unconditional moral approval.

questions.correctOption: Culture is transmitted socially and can be adapted through changing technologies.
questions.independentReview: Identified neighbor/apprentice teaching as social transmission and the new tool as adaptation. No claim that every technological change preserves all meanings or that cultural continuity requires unchanged equipment.

questions.correctOption: The device represents a shared technology, and the rotation represents a learned social practice.
questions.independentReview: Separated a material technology from a social access practice while recognizing both as learned cultural expressions. Avoided environmental determinism and any assertion of biological inheritance.

questions.correctOption: Resources influence possibilities, while learned preferences and histories can produce different practices.
questions.independentReview: Held crop/soil conditions similar while varying learned preparation. This rejects one-to-one environmental determination without denying that ingredients constrain possibilities; no real group’s custom is invented.

questions.correctOption: How do participants describe the meal’s organization, meaning and place in daily life?
questions.independentReview: Inspected presuppositions in the wording rather than the meal itself. The neutral contextual question does not assume any practice is ethically beyond critique; it avoids embedding a cultural ranking in the data-collection prompt.

questions.correctOption: A transmitted practice can change some organizational features while retaining meaningful continuity.
questions.independentReview: Kept the scope of change limited to ticketing and continuity grounded in explicit transmission of songs/meanings. Did not claim that every festival innovation is harmless or that all aspects remain unchanged.

questions.correctOption: Cultural traits can cross state borders and need not make each country internally uniform.
questions.independentReview: Compared two spatial partitions: state boundaries and the observed trait distribution. Their mismatch is explicit; no complete culture or individual identity is inferred from one food practice.

questions.correctOption: A self-selected festival sample may overrepresent participants interested in the tradition.
questions.independentReview: Identified selection into festival attendance and volunteering as possible overrepresentation of the trait. The conclusion fails because its population scope exceeds the sample, not because qualitative interviews are inherently invalid.
